title: Designing a Stack That Tracks the Minimum

phrases.explanation: Performing an operation in O(1), meaning it takes the same amount of time regardless of input size
Built above or in addition to something else, often referring to layering functionality
To maintain or record information as it changes over time
At any moment during the process or execution
A situation where you accept a cost in one area to gain a benefit in another

technical_terms.definition: A last-in, first-out data structure that supports push and pop operations
An additional data structure used alongside the main one to store helper information
A stack where elements are maintained in a sorted order, either increasing or decreasing
A condition that remains true throughout the execution of an algorithm
The average time per operation over a sequence of operations, even if some individual operations are costly

java_methods.description: Creates a new empty stack of integers
Pushes an element onto the top of the stack
Removes and returns the element on top of the stack
Returns the top element without removing it
Returns the smaller of two integer values

concept: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element, all in constant time.

solutions.label: Brute Force Scan
solutions.time_complexity: O(n) for getMin, O(1) for others
solutions.summary: Use a regular stack and scan all elements each time getMin is called.

solutions.label: Two-Stack Approach
solutions.summary: Maintain a second stack that tracks the current minimum at each level of the main stack.

solutions.label: Single Stack with Pairs
solutions.summary: Store each element alongside its current minimum as a pair in one stack, eliminating the need for a separate structure.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style A fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    style B fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    style C fill:#f87171,color:#fff
    A["push 5"] --> B["push 3"]
    B --> C["push 7"]
    C --> D["getMin → 3"]
    D --> E["pop → 7"]
    E --> F["getMin → 3"]
    F --> G["pop → 3"]
    G --> H["getMin → 5"]

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's today's problem. I'd like you to design a special stack. It should support the usual push, pop, and top operations, but also a getMin operation that returns the smallest element currently in the stack. The key constraint is that all four operations must run in constant time.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Interesting. So push, pop, and top behave like a normal stack, and getMin returns the minimum among all elements still in the stack. Can I assume all values are integers?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, all values are integers, and they can be negative. You can also assume pop, top, and getMin will never be called on an empty stack.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Good. What if we push duplicate values, like pushing three twice? And is there a limit on the number of operations?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Duplicates are allowed. The number of operations can be up to thirty thousand, so efficiency matters.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Let me confirm. If I push five, then three, then seven, getMin returns three. If I pop seven and call getMin again, it still returns three. Then if I pop three, getMin should return five. The minimum updates dynamically as elements are removed. Let me think about approaches.

sections.title: Brute Force Scan
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style S1 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S2 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style S3 fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style SCAN fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    S1["Stack: 5, 3, 7"] --> SCAN["getMin: scan all → 3"]
    S2["Pop 7 → Stack: 5, 3"] --> SCAN2["getMin: scan all → 3"]
    S3["Pop 3 → Stack: 5"] --> SCAN3["getMin: scan all → 5"]

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The simplest approach is to use a regular stack for push, pop, and top, all in O of one. For getMin, I scan every element in the stack to find the smallest value. This takes O of n time where n is the number of elements.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Can you walk through our example? Push five, push three, push seven, then call getMin.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: After pushing five, three, and seven, the stack holds those three values. When getMin is called, I iterate through all three and find that three is the smallest. If I pop seven and call getMin again, I scan five and three, still returning three.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: This works but getMin is O of n. The problem requires constant time for all operations. Can you do better?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Right. The bottleneck is recalculating the minimum from scratch each time. I need a way to keep track of the minimum as elements are pushed and popped, so I can retrieve it instantly.

sections.title: Two-Stack Approach
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style M1 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style M2 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style M3 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style N1 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style N2 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style N3 fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    subgraph Main Stack
        M1["5"] --> M2["3"] --> M3["7"]
    end
    subgraph Min Stack
        N1["5"] --> N2["3"] --> N3["3"]
    end
    M3 -.->|"getMin = top of Min Stack"| N3

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I'll use two stacks. The main stack stores all elements normally. The second stack, called the min stack, tracks the running minimum. When I push a value, I also push the smaller of that value and the current min stack top onto the min stack.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Let me trace through the example. I push five. Main stack has five, min stack has five. I push three. Main stack has five, three. Since three is less than five, min stack gets three. I push seven. Main stack has five, three, seven. Seven is greater than three, so min stack gets three again.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Now what happens when you pop?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I pop from both stacks simultaneously. Popping removes seven from the main stack and three from the min stack. The min stack top is now three, so getMin still returns three. If I pop again, both stacks lose three, and the min stack top is five. Every operation is O of one.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great. The time complexity is O of one for all operations, and space is O of n since the min stack mirrors the main stack in size. Can we reduce the space overhead at all?

sections.title: Single Stack with Pairs
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    style P1 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style P2 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    style P3 fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    P1["(5, min=5)"] --> P2["(3, min=3)"] --> P3["(7, min=3)"]
    P3 -.->|"getMin → read min from top pair → 3"| R["Result: 3"]
    style R fill:#fb923c,color:#fff

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Instead of two separate stacks, I can store pairs in a single stack. Each entry holds the value and the current minimum at that point. This eliminates the overhead of managing two structures.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Walking through the example again. Push five: I store the pair five, five since five is the only element. Push three: three is less than five, so I store three, three. Push seven: seven is greater than three, so I store seven, three.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: And getMin just reads the second value from the top pair?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Exactly. The top pair is seven, three, so getMin returns three. When I pop, I remove the entire pair. The new top is three, three, and getMin returns three. Pop again, the top is five, five, and getMin returns five. All operations are O of one, and we use a single stack.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: The space is still O of n since we store an extra value per element, but the implementation is cleaner. Well done.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    style A fill:#60a5fa,color:#fff
    style B fill:#a78bfa,color:#fff
    style C fill:#fb923c,color:#fff
    A["Brute Force
getMin: O of n
Space: O of n"] --> B["Two-Stack
All ops: O of 1
Space: O of n"]
    B --> C["Pairs in One Stack
All ops: O of 1
Space: O of n, simpler"]

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: To summarize, the brute force scans all elements for getMin at O of n cost. The two-stack approach achieves O of one for every operation by maintaining a parallel min stack. The single stack with pairs provides the same O of one performance with a simpler implementation.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: The key insight is that the minimum only changes when we push or pop, so we can record it alongside each element. This pattern of caching derived state at each level of a stack is useful in many related problems.
